To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

generalized inferences from comparison group studies (i.e., nonrandomized comparisons) are biased by differences between the study sites and the inference sites in average performance and in average impact, that covariate adjustment reduces bias, and that criteria for bias reduction in past studies apply to generalized inference.

generalized impact estimates based on CGS are biased by differences between study and inference sites, that covariate adjustment can reduce but not completely eliminate this bias, and that criteria for bias reduction in past studies extend to the generalized inference context.

(1) generalized inferences from comparison-group studies (CGS) are biased, and that (2) the bias is reduced when researchers use the same covariates that are used for covariate adjustment in the CGS, and when the inference site is similar to the study site.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accuracy of generalized impact estimates from CGSs.
bias in causal inference from nonrandomized comparison group studies.
how well CGSs work in practice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this article provides a within-study comparison approach for evaluating bias in generalized causal inferences from CGSI.
the results of the study are consistent with the findings of other studies and that they can be generalized with confidence to similar settings.

the results of the study provide evidence that the use of covariates to adjust for differences in average impact and average performance can reduce the bias in generalized causal inferences from CG studies, but the reduction is not complete and is dependent on the strength of the covariates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of comparison group studies to estimate impacts and generalize to other settings is a reasonable strategy, but one that should be used with caution and in the context of other information.
the results from CGSs can be generalized to other settings with a degree of confidence.
CGSs are useful for making causal inferences, but the validity of generalized causal inferences is more limited than for site-specific causal inferences.
The main takeaway from our work is that
researchers and policymakers should be cautious when generalizing from CGSs.
researchers should be aware that bias from differences between study and inference sites may be a factor in the validity of generalized impact estimates based on CGS.
CGSs can be used for generalization when the study and inference contexts are similar.
